newsitem.title: INDIA: India 96/97 industry growth seen slowing to 8 pct.
newsitem.headline: India 96/97 industry growth seen slowing to 8 pct.

text.p: Indian industrial growth will slow to eight percent in 1996/97 (April-March) handicapped by falling demand, high borrowing costs and political uncertainty, business leaders said on Sunday.
This compares with an official industrial growth target of 12 percent for the fiscal year ending March 31, after the country notched 12.1 percent in 1995/96.

"Industry will grow at less than 10 percent in the current year. In fact we will be lucky to have eight percent growth," V. Raghuraman, secretary general of Associated Chambers of Commerce (Assocham), told Reuters.
Overall industry growth was 6.4 percent between April and August compared to 13.2 percent in the same period last year.
Lack of domestic demand for output, rising inventories, infrastructure bottlenecks and political uncertainty would retard industrial growth, business leaders said.

"We are looking at an optimistic figure of eight percent assuming that demand shortfall will improve due to actions of the government," Amit Mitra, secretary general of the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry, told Reuters.
A recent survey by the Confederation of Indian Industries (CII) showed that 57 percent of the 361 companies participating in the poll forecast industrial growth to be about 10 percent.
Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda will meet industry and trade bodies on December 31 to discuss ways to boost growth.
"We hope this meeting will result in concrete ideas in consultation with industry," Mitra said.
The industry officials said a first step should be to scrap the controversial minimum alternate tax (MAT) on companies.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram has already indicated that the unpopular MAT will be removed once the government aligns domestic company and income tax laws in the next fiscal year.
The industry leaders said that while the availability of bank funds to the industry had increased in recent months, interest rates were still too high.
Despite an average inflation rate of about six percent in the past six months, prime lending rates range between 14.5 and 15 percent.
A depressed domestic stock market has further prevented the industry from raising funds for expansion and modernisation, officials said.
"The government borrowing in the market is crowding out the private sector. Many corporates have put investment plans on hold," Raghuraman said.
Earlier this month Reserve Bank of India (RBI) governor C. Rangarajan said he expected industrial growth to pick up in the second half of the fiscal year and the flow of bank funds to improve.
The RBI is expected to make two half-percentage point cuts in banks' cash reserve requirement to 10 percent in January.
Industry leaders also cited worries over the stability of Deve Gowda's fragile 13-party centre-left coalition as a factor hurting confidence and slowing growth.
"There are conflicting signals from different quarters within the government. The government speaks in different voices," said an industrialist, who did not want to be named.
